title: IronPeak Systems - Inference routing and p95 targets discovery
header: Date: 2026-07-08 09:00 PDT | Duration: ~54m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Rajiv Patel (CTO, IronPeak), Sofia Gomez (Lead ML Eng), Tom Reed (Infra Eng). Recording: Fireflies.ai auto-transcript. Location: Zoom.
summary: Intro + qualification -> deep dive on p95 latency targets and streaming token/sec expectations -> hosted vs dedicated vs private decision factors (latency, caching, KV cache behavior, quantization) -> benchmark ask and next steps. Customer needs p95<=250ms for short turn responses and predictable capacity for peak spikes. Action: run token/sec streaming bench & share security pack.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'll do a quick intro from redwood then pass to liam for the technical deep dive. um, is this time still good for you all?
[00:10] Rajiv Patel: yeah thanks Maya, loud and clear. we wanted to use this to validate p95 targets and get a sense of economics across hosted/dedicated/private options.
[00:18] Sofia Gomez: hi, i'll be driving most of the technical questions. our main goal is to support a customer-facing chat assistant with streaming responses. p95 needs to be under ~250ms for short responses (100-200 tokens) and for longer outputs we want consistent tail behavior.
[00:30] Liam Ortiz: great, thanks. quick clarifying Qs: what's your expected concurrency at peak and typical tokens/sec per session?
[00:38] Tom Reed: at peak we estimate 400 concurrent users hitting the model with about 30 requests/sec, average 90 tokens per request, but token bursts can go to 600-800 tokens for longer responses. our SLA demands p95 for the first 200 tokens ideally.
[00:50] Maya Chen: cool, that helps. do you currently host models yourselves or are you using a managed API?
[00:55] Rajiv Patel: currently hybrid—we run some lightweight models on prem for compliance and use public APIs for heavier workloads. but running larger models in-house has been painful. looking at redwood as a unified path that gives us both predictability and the option to move sensitive workloads privately.
[01:10] Liam Ortiz: got it. for p95 <250ms with streaming on ~100-200 tokens, two levers matter: model variant and serving mode (dedicated GPU pools vs hosted). also batching behavior and prefix/KV caching will change effective throughput.
[01:25] Sofia Gomez: we've found prefix reuse is huge; many conversations start with the same system prompt and user context, so any caching would help a lot. how mature is redwood's kv cache and prefix caching?
[01:34] Liam Ortiz: we have an automatic prefix caching layer in the runtime—it's not perfect in the transcript sorry—uh, the KV cache stores activations per session when appropriate. it reduces token compute for repeated prefixes. in dedicated deployments we can pin cache locality to GPUs to avoid cross-host hops. in hosted mode it's available but subject to eviction policies under heavy load.
[01:52] Tom Reed: eviction policies—what controls those? is it LRU, time-based, or by memory pressure?
[01:58] Liam Ortiz: mostly LRU plus memory-pressure heuristics, and you can set TTLs in Dedicated. in Private we can tune eviction aggressively to keep your working set resident.
[02:08] Rajiv Patel: latency wise, how do you get down to 200ms? we're worried about attention kernels and long contexts.
[02:14] Liam Ortiz: kernel selection + quantization profiles. for shorter tokens we pick optimized attention kernels and use int8/4 quantization where quality permits. also continuous batching can be tuned—if you enable micro-batching you trade a few ms for higher throughput. since you want p95 strict, we recommend Dedicated low-latency pool with small batch sizes and no micro-batching for customer-facing streaming.
[02:36] Sofia Gomez: ok, what's realistic token/sec per GPU for the models we're considering? we're evaluating an open LLM ~13B and also a trimmed 7B for latency-sensitive endpoints.
[02:45] Liam Ortiz: rough numbers: for 7B in int8 streaming you might see 600-1200 tokens/sec sustained depending on sequence length and kernels; 13B will be lower, maybe 200-450 tokens/sec sustained. those are ballpark—real numbers depend on sequence length, top-k sampling parameters, and whether KV cache hits.
[03:03] Rajiv Patel: hmm, to meet our 400 concurrent users at 30 rps, what's that translate to?
[03:08] Liam Ortiz: quick calc—if average req is 90 tokens and 400 concurrent with 30 rps, you'd need to model request concurrency differently. but roughly: tokens per second demand = 30 rps * 90 tokens = 2700 tokens/sec average. with a 7B at 1000 tokens/sec you'd need ~3 GPUs steady state, with headroom for burst maybe 5+ and autoscale. 13B at 300 tokens/sec would need ~9 GPUs steady state. this is simplified—real deployment tweaks (batching, cache) can reduce that need.
[03:36] Tom Reed: ok that math helps. can we run a redwood-provided token/sec benchmark with our prompt set? we want apples-to-apples.
[03:43] Maya Chen: absolutely. next step is Liam runs a tokenburst benchmark against a hosted sandbox and we run a dedicated bench if you want on-prem sim. we'll need your sample prompts and representative concurrency pattern.
[03:53] Sofia Gomez: we'll share a 1k sample prompt distribution and a histogram of token lengths. expect that in a day.
[03:58] Rajiv Patel: security: we need SOC2, SSO (SAML/Okta), KMS for key management, and audit logs retained for 1 year. how does redwood support that across hosting modes?
[04:10] Liam Ortiz: hosted supports SOC2 and SAML; KMS for key encryption at rest is available via provider-managed keys, and audit logs are on by default with configurable retention. Dedicated and Private give you more control—Private lets you bring your own KMS/HSM and keep logs in your VPC. i'll flag that in the security pack.
[04:26] Tom Reed: good. what about multi-region failover? we need <500ms region-to-region failover for availability.
[04:33] Liam Ortiz: smart routing can route by policy and we have warm standby replicas. failover adds latency initially but we can route to fallback smaller models to keep responses online while warm-up happens.
[04:44] Sofia Gomez: can redwood do model-family fallbacks automatically? e.g., degrade from 13B to 7B under pressure?
[04:49] Maya Chen: yes — rollout policies and fallback rules can downgrade to compatible model variants automatically based on capacity or latency policies.
[04:55] Rajiv Patel: pricing sensitivity—how should we think about unit economics for hosted vs dedicated?
[05:00] Maya Chen: hosted is pay-as-you-go but can have higher per-token unit cost. Dedicated is reserved capacity with lower unit cost at steady state but requires commit. Private has platform licensing plus infra. we'll share a tailored cost projection after we get your token distribution.
[05:14] Liam Ortiz: another important note: streaming SLOs are influenced by network RTT and connection multiplexing. if your apps open a new connection per request you'll pay a lot in overhead; we recommend long-lived streaming connections.
[05:26] Tom Reed: we currently multiplex with short-lived websockets, need to revisit.
[05:30] Sofia Gomez: on benchmarks—can you run both p95 latency and p95 token generation time? we want p95 time-to-first-token and p95 overall for 200 tokens.
[05:39] Liam Ortiz: yes we can measure ttf-token and p95 total for N tokens. our bench infra reports p50/p95/p99 and token/sec. we'll run both with your prompts.
[05:46] Rajiv Patel: sample acceptance criteria: p95 <=250ms for first-token at 100-200 tokens and p95 overall <=700ms for 600 tokens. are those doable?
[05:55] Liam Ortiz: with Dedicated low-latency config and 7B int8 maybe; 13B will be challenging for first-token under 250ms at high concurrency without scale. we should validate with bench.
[06:06] Maya Chen: cool —any other blockers?
[06:09] Sofia Gomez: one more, how determinisitc is cache behavior across restarts? we need cold-start behavior documented, and how long warm caches survive maintenance.
[06:18] Liam Ortiz: cold-starts clear local GPU cache; in Dedicated we replicate warm caches across a small pool to reduce cold-start impact during maintenance windows. we'll document cold vs warm latency numbers in the bench report.
[06:30] Tom Reed: great. last Q: any compliance for data residency in eu? we have EMEA customers.
[06:36] Maya Chen: yes we have region-specific hosting and can keep data-in-region for Private and Dedicated; hosted also has region selection but with multi-tenant limitations.
[06:44] Rajiv Patel: ok let's recap next steps.
[06:46] Maya Chen: recap: (1) IronPeak to share 1k sample prompts, token length histogram, and concurrency pattern (Sofia) — by 2026-07-09. (2) Liam to run hosted token/sec + p95 bench with those prompts and share raw bench csv and summary — target 2026-07-13. (3) Maya to send pricing draft + security pack (SOC2 cert, SAML guide, KMS options) — target 2026-07-12. (4) Schedule follow-up PoC planning meeting for week of 2026-07-20.
[07:12] Sofia Gomez: yes that timeline works. thanks all.
[07:15] Maya Chen: thanks, we'll follow up in email with links. shared artifacts: bench template (https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/token-bench-template.csv), security pack (https://redwood.ai/security/ironpeak-pack.pdf), and rough cost sheet (https://redwood.ai/pricing/estimate-ironpeak-2026.xlsx).
[07:30] Rajiv Patel: thanks, chat later.
[07:33] TRANSCRIPT NOTES: ASR imperfect in places ("KV cash" vs "KV cache" transcription). speaker overlaps at 03:03 - 03:08. recordings clipped briefly at 04:00 for ~3s (network).
